vo.text: Most email finders guess a pattern, call it verified, and hope it doesn't bounce.
This one gathers evidence, and never claims more than it found.

scenes.title: Email Finder
scenes.tagline: A name and a company website in. A work email out — with how much to trust it.

vo.text: Give it a name and a company website, and it works out the person's email, and how sure it can be.

scenes.headline: Free evidence first. [Pay only if you must.]
bullets: DNS, site crawl, sitemaps, GitHub authors
Linked PDFs and the Internet Archive
Search, a browser and mail verification only when needed

lines.text: T1 crawl · sitemap · GitHub  2 name/address pairs   free
T2 linked PDFs ............ staff directory   free
T6 catch-all? no → ladder: alex.rivera@ accepted

vo.text: It works through seven tiers of evidence. DNS, a relevance-scored crawl, sitemaps, GitHub commit authors, linked PDFs and the Internet Archive are all free, and they run first.
Search, a browser for blocked pages, and mail-server verification cost money, so they only run when the free tiers can't settle it.

scenes.headline: Published, deliverable and predicted are [three different claims.]
bullets: Deliverable: a mail server accepted it

items.title: confirmed
items.sub: published and accepted by the mail server

items.title: high
items.sub: verified deliverable, or a well-corroborated pattern

items.title: medium · low
items.sub: pattern from limited evidence · statistical prior

items.title: withheld
items.sub: on the suppression list (stored as SHA-256)

items.title: fail
items.sub: every candidate verifiably rejected — don't mail

vo.text: Results keep three claims apart, because they fail in different ways. Published means it was found on a page. Deliverable means a mail server accepted it. Predicted means a pattern produced it.
Only published and deliverable together earns confirmed, and catch-all domains are detected first, because a yes from them means nothing.

scenes.headline: A web app, a worker, and [RLS that actually works.]

nodes.title: Worker
nodes.sub: Drains the queue; waits for the DB

vo.text: It runs as a Next.js web app and a separate worker on Railway. A batch upload becomes one job per row, and the worker drains them.
I found that Drizzle was creating row-level security policies with no condition at all, which quietly made every row visible, so the real policies now live in SQL that runs after every push.
Read the full case study, and see how it was built.
